title: Distinct differences bound
q:
A set $A$ of positive integers is a Sidon set if all sums $a+b$ with $a\le b$ and $a,b\in A$ are distinct.

Let $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be a Sidon set. Show that the positive differences $a-a'$ with $a,a'\in A$, $a>a'$, are pairwise distinct, and deduce that $|A|<\sqrt{2N}+1$.
source: Elementary counting (proof checked by the reviewer); see K. O'Bryant, A complete annotated bibliography of work related to Sidon sequences, Electron. J. Combin. Dynamic Survey DS11 (2004), arXiv:math/0407117
note: The trivial upper bound; the whole of Erdős #30 is about replacing $\sqrt{2N}$ by $\sqrt N$ plus the smallest possible error.

title: The greedy Sidon sequence grows at most cubically
q:
Let $a_1=1$ and, for $n\ge1$, let $a_{n+1}$ be the least integer greater than $a_n$ such that $\{a_1,\ldots,a_{n+1}\}$ is a Sidon set.

Show that $a_{n+1}\le 4n^3$ for every $n\ge1$, and deduce that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that the infinite Sidon set $A=\{a_1,a_2,\ldots\}$ satisfies $|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|\ge cN^{1/3}$ for all $N\ge1$.
source: A. M. Mian and S. Chowla, Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. India Sect. A 14 (1944) (the sequence); the cubic bound $a_n\le(n-1)^3+1$ is in A. Stöhr, J. Reine Angew. Math. 194 (1955), see O'Bryant, Electron. J. Combin. Dynamic Survey DS11 (2004) and J. Cilleruelo, Infinite Sidon sequences, arXiv:1209.0326
note: This is the greedy (Mian–Chowla) sequence of Erdős #340; this trivial $N^{1/3}$ bound is still the best known lower bound for it, against the conjectured $N^{1/2-\varepsilon}$.

title: The Erdős–Turán quadratic-residue construction
q:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and, for $0\le k<p$, let $r_k\in\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\}$ be the residue of $k^2$ modulo $p$. Show that
$$A_p=\{\,2pk+r_k : 0\le k<p\,\}$$
is a Sidon set of $p$ elements contained in $\{0,1,\ldots,2p^2-1\}$.

Deduce, using that the ratio of consecutive primes tends to $1$, that the maximum size $h(N)$ of a Sidon set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfies $h(N)\ge(1/\sqrt2-o(1))\sqrt N$.
source: P. Erdős and P. Turán, On a problem of Sidon in additive number theory, and on some related problems, J. London Math. Soc. 16 (1941), 212–215
note: The first algebraic construction: it shows $h(N)$ really has order $\sqrt N$, leaving only the constant and the error term.

title: Lindström's upper bound
q:
Show that every Sidon set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfies
$$|A|<N^{1/2}+N^{1/4}+1.$$
source: B. Lindström, An inequality for B2-sequences, J. Combinatorial Theory 6 (1969), 211–212; the bound $\sqrt N+O(N^{1/4})$ goes back to Erdős and Turán (1941)
note: Counting differences in short windows replaces $\sqrt{2N}$ by $\sqrt N$; the $N^{1/4}$ error term is the barrier Erdős #30 asks to break.

title: Singer difference sets give asymptotically optimal Sidon sets
q:
Let $q$ be a prime power. Show that there exist $q+1$ residues modulo $m=q^2+q+1$ such that every nonzero residue modulo $m$ is a difference of two of them in exactly one way.

Deduce that $h(q^2+q+1)\ge q+1$, where $h(N)$ is the maximum size of a Sidon subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and, using that consecutive primes $p<p'$ satisfy $p'/p\to1$ together with the upper bound of the previous problem, that $h(N)=(1+o(1))\sqrt N$.
source: J. Singer, A theorem in finite projective geometry and some applications to number theory, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 43 (1938), 377–385
note: Matches the upper bound to first order; at $N=q^2+q+1$ it gives $h(N)\ge\sqrt N+1/2-o(1)$, and Green's Problem 31 asks whether one can beat $\sqrt N+O(1)$ even for infinitely many $N$.

title: B3 sets: counting bound and the Bose–Chowla construction
q:
Call $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ a $B_3$ set if the sums $a+b+c$ with $a\le b\le c$ and $a,b,c\in A$ are all distinct, and let $f(N)$ be the maximum size of a $B_3$ set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

(a) By counting the sums, show that $f(N)<(18N)^{1/3}$.

(b) Show that for every prime power $q$ there is a $B_3$ set of $q$ integers contained in $\{1,\ldots,q^3-1\}$, and deduce that $f(N)\ge(1-o(1))N^{1/3}$.
source: R. C. Bose and S. Chowla, Theorems in the additive theory of numbers, Comment. Math. Helv. 37 (1962/63), 141–147; the counting bound $(h\cdot h!)^{1/h}N^{1/h}$ is classical, see O'Bryant, Electron. J. Combin. Dynamic Survey DS11 (2004)
note: Gives the right order $N^{1/3}$ for triple sums; Erdős #241 asks whether the lower bound is asymptotically sharp, which needs an upper bound of the form $(1+o(1))N^{1/3}$.

title: Infinite Sidon sets cannot be dense at every scale
q:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ be an infinite Sidon set. Show that there is an absolute constant $C$ (independent of $A$) such that
$$\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{\sqrt{x/\log x}}\le C.$$
In particular $\liminf_{x\to\infty}|A\cap[1,x]|/\sqrt x=0$.
source: Erdős; proof in A. Stöhr, Gelöste und ungelöste Fragen über Basen der natürlichen Zahlenreihe II, J. Reine Angew. Math. 194 (1955), and in Halberstam & Roth, Sequences, Vol. I (1966), Ch. II; see also erdosproblems.com/1191 and O'Bryant, Electron. J. Combin. Dynamic Survey DS11 (2004)
note: An infinite Sidon set must be thinner than finite optimal ones infinitely often; Erdős #1191 asks whether the constant $C$ can be replaced by $0$.

title: Maximal Sidon sets: the cube-root bound and Ruzsa's construction
q:
A Sidon set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is maximal if $A\cup\{x\}$ is not a Sidon set for every $x\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus A$.

(a) Show that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that every maximal Sidon set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has $|A|\ge cN^{1/3}$.

(b) Show that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every large $N$ there is a maximal Sidon set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $|A|\le C(N\log N)^{1/3}$.
source: Part (a): elementary counting, stated as easy in erdosproblems.com/156; the question comes from P. Erdős, A. Sárközy and V. T. Sós, On sum sets of Sidon sets I, J. Number Theory 47 (1994), 329–347. Part (b): I. Z. Ruzsa, A small maximal Sidon set, Ramanujan J. 2 (1998), 55–58
note: The two bounds differ only by $(\log N)^{1/3}$; Erdős #156 asks whether that logarithm can be removed.

title: Ruzsa's dense infinite Sidon sequence
q:
Show that there is an infinite Sidon set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ such that for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|\ge N^{\sqrt2-1-\varepsilon}$$
for all sufficiently large $N$.
source: I. Z. Ruzsa, An infinite Sidon sequence, J. Number Theory 68 (1998), 63–71
note: Improves the greedy exponent $1/3$ (and Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi's $(N\log N)^{1/3}$, 1981) to $\sqrt2-1\approx0.414$; Erdős #39 asks for every exponent below $1/2$.

title: Balogh–Füredi–Roy: improving the constant in the N^{1/4} term
q:
Show that for all sufficiently large $N$, every Sidon set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfies
$$|A|\le\sqrt N+0.998\,N^{1/4}.$$
source: J. Balogh, Z. Füredi and S. Roy, An upper bound on the size of Sidon sets, Amer. Math. Monthly 130 (2023), no. 5, 437–445; arXiv:2103.15850
note: The first improvement of the constant $1$ in Lindström's $N^{1/4}$ term in over fifty years; Erdős #30 asks to lower the exponent $1/4$ itself to any $\varepsilon>0$.

title: The representation function is never eventually constant
q: Let $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ be infinite and let $r(n)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2: a\le b,\ a+b=n\}$ count representations with $a\le b$. Show that $r(n)$ is not constant for all sufficiently large $n$.
source: G. A. Dirac, Note on a problem in additive number theory, J. London Math. Soc. 26 (1951), 312–313; see M. B. Nathanson, Inverse problems for representation functions in additive number theory, arXiv:0712.0408, Theorem 1
note: The weakest form of the Erdős–Turán philosophy that a representation function cannot be too regular.

title: A basis of order two has at least square-root growth
q:
Let $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ be such that every sufficiently large integer can be written as $a+b$ with $a,b\in A$. Show that
$$\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap\{0,1,\ldots,N\}|}{\sqrt N}\ge\sqrt2.$$
source: Elementary counting (proof checked by the reviewer); the order of magnitude $A(x)\gg\sqrt x$ for bases of order $2$ is Theorem 1 of M. B. Nathanson, Cassels bases, arXiv:0905.3144
note: Shows a basis of order $2$ has on average at least a constant number of representations, the starting point of the Erdős–Turán conjecture.

title: A thin basis from binary digits
q: Let $E$ be the set of nonnegative integers whose binary expansion uses only the powers $4^j$ ($j\ge0$), and let $O=2E$ be the set of those using only the powers $2\cdot4^j$. Show that $A=E\cup O$ satisfies $A+A\supseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and $|A\cap\{0,1,\ldots,N\}|\le4\sqrt N$ for every $N\ge1$.
source: D. Raikov (1937) and A. Stöhr (1937); see M. B. Nathanson, Cassels bases, arXiv:0905.3144, where the bound $A(x)<(2+\sqrt2)\sqrt x$ is shown
note: The square-root lower bound is attained up to a constant, so the Erdős–Turán conjecture cannot follow from counting alone; in this example $r(n)$ is unbounded.

title: Schnirelmann's inequality
q:
For $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ let $A(n)=\#\{a\in A:1\le a\le n\}$ and define the Schnirelmann density $\sigma(A)=\inf_{n\ge1}A(n)/n$.

(a) Show that if $0\in A$ and $0\in B$ then $\sigma(A+B)\ge\sigma(A)+\sigma(B)-\sigma(A)\sigma(B)$.

(b) Deduce that if $0\in A$ and $\sigma(A)>0$, then $A$ is a basis of finite order: there is $h$ such that every nonnegative integer is a sum of $h$ elements of $A$.
source: L. G. Schnirelmann (1930); M. B. Nathanson, Additive Number Theory: The Classical Bases, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 164, Springer (1996)
note: The basic density-increment inequality for sumsets, the tool behind Schnirelmann's proof that the primes form a basis of finite order.

title: Erdős's covering-congruence obstruction for 2^k + p
q:
(a) Show that every integer $k$ lies in at least one of the residue classes $0 \bmod 2$, $0 \bmod 3$, $1 \bmod 4$, $3 \bmod 8$, $7 \bmod 12$, $23 \bmod 24$.

(b) Prove that there is an infinite arithmetic progression of odd positive integers none of which can be written as $2^k+p$ with $k\ge0$ an integer and $p$ a prime.
source: P. Erdős, On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems, Summa Brasil. Math. 2 (1950), 113–123
note: Contrasts with Romanoff's theorem (1934) that the integers $2^k+p$ have positive lower density; Erdős #16 asks whether such progressions explain all exceptions.

title: Erdős's density increment for adding a basis
q:
Let $\sigma$ denote Schnirelmann density, $\sigma(A)=\inf_{n\ge1}\#\{a\in A:1\le a\le n\}/n$. Let $B\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ with $0\in B$ be a basis of order $k$, i.e. every nonnegative integer is a sum of $k$ elements of $B$. Let $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ with $0\in A$ and $\alpha=\sigma(A)$. Show that
$$\sigma(A+B)\ge\alpha+\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{2k}.$$
source: P. Erdős, On the arithmetical density of the sum of two sequences, one of which forms a basis for the integers, Acta Arith. 1 (1936), 197–200
note: This is Erdős #35 with $2k$ in place of $k$; the sharper form follows from Plünnecke's inequality $\sigma(A+B)\ge\alpha^{1-1/k}$ (J. Reine Angew. Math. 243, 1970), since $\alpha^{1-1/k}\ge\alpha+\alpha(1-\alpha)/k$.

title: A basis of order two with logarithmically many representations
q:
Let $r(n)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:a+b=n\}$. Show that there exist $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and constants $0<c_1<c_2$ such that
$$c_1\log n\le r(n)\le c_2\log n$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.
source: P. Erdős, Problems and results in additive number theory, Colloque sur la Théorie des Nombres, Bruxelles 1955, CBRM (1956), 127–137 (the upper bound alone is in P. Erdős, On a problem of Sidon in additive number theory, Acta Sci. Math. (Szeged) 15 (1954), 255–259); extended to every order $h$ by P. Erdős and P. Tetali, Representations of integers as the sum of k terms, Random Structures Algorithms 1 (1990), 245–261
note: Shows the conjectured growth $\log n$ in the strong Erdős–Turán conjecture is attainable; Erdős #66 asks whether $r(n)/\log n$ can even converge to a nonzero limit.

title: Bases of order two have a representation count of at least 8 infinitely often
q: Let $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and $r(n)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:a+b=n\}$ (ordered pairs). Suppose $r(n)\ge1$ for every integer $n\ge0$. Show that $r(n)\ge8$ for infinitely many $n$.
source: P. Borwein, S. Choi and F. Chu, An old conjecture of Erdős–Turán on additive bases, Math. Comp. 75 (2006), 475–484; improving the bound 6 of G. Grekos, L. Haddad, C. Helou and J. Pihko, On the Erdős–Turán conjecture, J. Number Theory 102 (2003), 339–352
note: The best known constant lower bound on $\limsup r(n)$; Erdős #28 asks for $\limsup r(n)=\infty$.

title: The Erdős–Fuchs theorem
q:
Let $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ be infinite and let $R(N)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:a+b\le N\}$. Show that for no constant $c>0$ can one have
$$R(N)=cN+o\!\left(N^{1/4}(\log N)^{-1/2}\right)\quad(N\to\infty).$$
source: P. Erdős and W. H. J. Fuchs, On a problem of additive number theory, J. London Math. Soc. 31 (1956), 67–73
note: Quantifies that the representation function cannot be regular on average, answering a question of Erdős and Turán about $R(N)=cN+O(1)$; the analytic method is a model for attacks on the irregularity problems around Erdős #28 and #66.

title: Gallagher: a prime plus boundedly many powers of 2
source: P. X. Gallagher, Primes and powers of 2, Invent. Math. 29 (1975), 125–142
note: The density version of Erdős #10; the open problem asks for a single $k$ that represents all large integers.

title: Van der Waerden number W(3,2)
q: Show that every colouring of $\{1,2,\ldots,9\}$ with two colours contains a monochromatic $3$-term arithmetic progression, and that this fails for $\{1,2,\ldots,8\}$.
source: R. L. Graham, B. L. Rothschild and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey Theory (2nd ed., 1990)
note: The smallest nontrivial case of van der Waerden's theorem, of which Szemerédi's theorem is the density version.

title: Monotone 3-term progressions in permutations
q:
A monotone $k$-term arithmetic progression in a sequence $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ is a choice of indices $i_1<\cdots<i_k$ such that $x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_k}$ is an arithmetic progression (increasing or decreasing).

(a) Show that for every $n\ge1$ there is a permutation of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with no monotone $3$-term arithmetic progression.

(b) Show that every permutation $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ of the positive integers contains a monotone $3$-term arithmetic progression.
source: J. A. Davis, R. C. Entringer, R. L. Graham and G. J. Simmons, On permutations containing no long arithmetic progressions, Acta Arith. 34 (1977), 81–90
note: The same paper constructs a permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ with no monotone $5$-term progression, leaving $4$ terms as Erdős #196.

title: A progression-free set from ternary digits
q: Let $r_3(N)$ be the maximum size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ containing no three distinct elements in arithmetic progression. Show that the set of $n\ge1$ such that $n-1$ has only digits $0$ and $1$ in base $3$ contains no $3$-term arithmetic progression, and deduce that $r_3(N)\ge\tfrac12N^{\log2/\log3}$ for all $N\ge1$.
source: P. Erdős and P. Turán, On some sequences of integers, J. London Math. Soc. 11 (1936), 261–264
note: The first construction in the paper that introduced $r_k(N)$; it shows progression-free sets can have polynomial size.

title: Behrend's construction
q:
Show that there is a constant $c>0$ such that for all $N\ge2$ there is a set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $3$-term arithmetic progression and
$$|A|\ge N\exp\!\left(-c\sqrt{\log N}\right).$$
source: F. A. Behrend, On sets of integers which contain no three terms in arithmetical progression, Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. USA 32 (1946), 331–332
note: Shows $r_3(N)=N^{1-o(1)}$, so any upper bound must leave room for this; it is still essentially the best lower bound.

title: Roth's theorem
q: Show that there is a constant $C$ such that for all $N\ge3$ every subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $3$-term arithmetic progression has at most $CN/\log\log N$ elements.
source: K. F. Roth, On certain sets of integers, J. London Math. Soc. 28 (1953), 104–109
note: The $k=3$ case of Erdős #139 by Fourier-analytic density increment, the method all later 3-AP bounds refine.

title: Szemerédi's theorem
q: Let $k\ge3$ and let $r_k(N)$ be the maximum size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $k$-term arithmetic progression. Show that $r_k(N)=o(N)$ as $N\to\infty$; equivalently, every subset of $\mathbb{N}$ of positive upper density contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.
source: E. Szemerédi, On sets of integers containing no k elements in arithmetic progression, Acta Arith. 27 (1975), 199–245
note: This is Erdős #139, now solved; Erdős #3 asks for arbitrarily long progressions under the much weaker hypothesis $\sum_{n\in A}1/n=\infty$, and all later work on it is about the rate in $r_k(N)=o(N)$.

title: Gowers's quantitative Szemerédi theorem
q: Let $k\ge3$ and $c_k=2^{-2^{k+9}}$. Show that for all sufficiently large $N$, every subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $k$-term arithmetic progression has at most $N(\log\log N)^{-c_k}$ elements.
source: W. T. Gowers, A new proof of Szemerédi's theorem, Geom. Funct. Anal. 11 (2001), 465–588
note: The first bound for all $k$ with a reasonable rate, introducing the Gowers uniformity norms.

title: Kelley–Meka bounds for 3-term progressions
q:
Show that there is a constant $c>0$ such that for all $N\ge3$ every subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $3$-term arithmetic progression has at most
$$N\exp\!\left(-c(\log N)^{1/12}\right)$$
elements. Deduce that every $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_{n\in A}1/n=\infty$ contains a $3$-term arithmetic progression.
source: Z. Kelley and R. Meka, Strong bounds for 3-progressions, FOCS 2023, arXiv:2302.05537 (the exponent $1/12$ is made explicit in T. F. Bloom and O. Sisask, The Kelley–Meka bounds for sets free of three-term arithmetic progressions, Essent. Number Theory 2 (2023), arXiv:2302.07211); exponent improved to $1/9$ by T. F. Bloom and O. Sisask, An improvement to the Kelley–Meka bounds on three-term arithmetic progressions, arXiv:2309.02353
note: Answers Green's Problem 9, gives a new proof of the $k=3$ case of Erdős #3 (first proved by Bloom and Sisask in 2020), and brings the upper bound to the same shape as Behrend's lower bound, with exponent $1/12$ against $1/2$.

title: Leng–Sah–Sawhney bounds for long progressions
q:
Let $k\ge5$. Show that there is a constant $c_k>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $N$, every subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $k$-term arithmetic progression has at most
$$N\exp\!\left(-(\log\log N)^{c_k}\right)$$
elements.
source: J. Leng, A. Sah and M. Sawhney, Improved bounds for Szemerédi's theorem, arXiv:2402.17995 (2024)
note: The first bound for $k\ge5$ beating every power of $\log\log N$; Erdős #3 for $k$-term progressions would follow from a bound $r_k(N)\ll N/(\log N)^{1+\delta}$ for some $\delta>0$.

title: The Green–Tao theorem
q: Show that for every $k\ge3$ the primes contain a $k$-term arithmetic progression.
source: B. Green and T. Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Ann. of Math. 167 (2008), 481–547
note: A relative Szemerédi theorem for the primes, which have density zero; Erdős #141 asks for such progressions among consecutive primes, and #200 for the length of the longest one below $N$.

title: Sumsets of integers: the trivial bound and its equality case
q:
Let $A$ be a finite nonempty set of integers and $A+A=\{a+b : a,b\in A\}$. Prove that $$|A+A|\ge 2|A|-1.$$

Show moreover that equality holds if and only if $A$ is an arithmetic progression.
source: M. B. Nathanson, Additive Number Theory: Inverse Problems and the Geometry of Sumsets, GTM 165, Springer (1996), Ch. 1
note: The simplest direct theorem together with its inverse theorem: extremal sumset size forces arithmetic structure.

title: The Cauchy–Davenport theorem
q: Let $p$ be a prime and let $A,B$ be nonempty subsets of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Prove that $$|A+B|\ge \min\big(p,\ |A|+|B|-1\big).$$
source: A.-L. Cauchy (1813); H. Davenport, On the addition of residue classes, J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935)
note: Transfers the integer bound to a cyclic group of prime order, where wrap-around is the only obstruction.

title: Ruzsa's triangle inequality
q:
Let $A,B,C$ be finite nonempty subsets of an abelian group. Prove that $$|A|\,|B-C|\le |A-B|\,|A-C|.$$

Deduce that $d(X,Y)=\log\dfrac{|X-Y|}{\sqrt{|X|\,|Y|}}$ satisfies $d(B,C)\le d(A,B)+d(A,C)$.
source: I. Z. Ruzsa (1978); T. Tao and V. Vu, Additive Combinatorics, Cambridge University Press (2006)
note: First tool for passing information about one sumset to another; an injection argument rather than a counting identity.

title: Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality
q: Let $A,B$ be finite nonempty subsets of an abelian group with $|A+B|\le K|A|$. Prove that for all integers $m,n\ge 0$ with $m+n\ge 1$, $$|mB-nB|\le K^{m+n}|A|,$$ where $mB-nB$ is the set of all $b_1+\cdots+b_m-b'_1-\cdots-b'_n$ with $b_i,b'_j\in B$.
source: G. Petridis, New proofs of Plünnecke-type estimates for product sets in groups, Combinatorica 32 (2012), 721–733 (inequality due to Plünnecke 1970 and Ruzsa 1989)
note: Small doubling propagates to all iterated sum and difference sets with polynomial loss; used in every Freiman-type theorem below.

title: Bogolyubov's lemma in the finite field model
q: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$ have density $\alpha=|A|/2^n>0$. Prove that $A+A+A+A$ contains a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ of codimension at most $\alpha^{-2}$.
source: N. N. Bogolyubov (1939); B. Green, Finite field models in additive combinatorics, Surveys in Combinatorics 2005, LMS Lecture Note Series 327, §10
note: The basic Fourier-analytic argument (large spectrum plus Parseval); Green's Problem 50 asks to improve the codimension from $\alpha^{-2}$ to $O(\log(1/\alpha))$.

title: The Erdős–Heilbronn conjecture for restricted sums
q: Let $p$ be a prime and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ be nonempty. Writing $A\hat{+}A=\{a+b : a,b\in A,\ a\neq b\}$, prove that $$|A\hat{+}A|\ge \min\big(p,\ 2|A|-3\big).$$
source: J. A. Dias da Silva and Y. O. Hamidoune, Cyclic spaces for Grassmann derivatives and additive theory, Bull. London Math. Soc. 26 (1994); polynomial-method proof: N. Alon, M. B. Nathanson and I. Z. Ruzsa, Adding distinct congruence classes modulo a prime, Amer. Math. Monthly 102 (1995)
note: Restricting to distinct summands breaks the Cauchy–Davenport proofs; the polynomial method handles it and settles Erdős Problem 476.

title: Freiman's 3k−4 theorem
q: Let $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ be finite with $|A|=k\ge 3$ and $$|A+A|\le 3k-4.$$ Prove that $A$ is contained in an arithmetic progression of length at most $|A+A|-k+1$.
source: G. A. Freiman (1959); see M. B. Nathanson, Additive Number Theory: Inverse Problems and the Geometry of Sumsets, GTM 165 (1996), Ch. 1
note: The first genuinely structural inverse theorem: doubling below 3 forces containment in a short progression.

title: Ruzsa's Freiman theorem in groups of exponent 2
q: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$ be nonempty with $|A+A|\le K|A|$. Prove that $A$ is contained in a subspace $H\le\mathbb{F}_2^n$ with $$|H|\le K^2\,2^{K^4}\,|A|.$$
source: I. Z. Ruzsa, An analog of Freiman's theorem in groups, Astérisque 258 (1999), 323–326 (proved there for groups of torsion $r$, with bound $K^2r^{K^4}|A|$)
note: Freiman's theorem in the model setting with an exponential loss in $K$; Marton's conjecture (Green's Problem 49) asks for polynomial loss.

title: Sanders' quasi-polynomial Bogolyubov lemma
q: Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that the following holds. If $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$ has density $\alpha>0$, then $A+A+A+A$ contains a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ of codimension at most $C\log^4(2/\alpha)$.
source: T. Sanders, On the Bogolyubov–Ruzsa lemma, Analysis & PDE 5 (2012), 627–655, arXiv:1011.0107 (Theorem A.1)
note: Replaces $\alpha^{-2}$ by a power of $\log(1/\alpha)$ via almost-periodicity; the conjectured codimension in Green's Problem 50 is $O(\log(1/\alpha))$.

title: Marton's conjecture (polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa) over F_2
q: Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ (one may take $C=12$) such that the following holds. If $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is nonempty with $|A+A|\le K|A|$, then $A$ is covered by at most $2K^{C}$ cosets of some subgroup $H\le\mathbb{F}_2^n$ with $|H|\le|A|$.
source: W. T. Gowers, B. Green, F. Manners and T. Tao, On a conjecture of Marton, Ann. of Math. 201 (2025), 515–549, arXiv:2311.05762 (2023)
note: Polynomial dependence on $K$, solving Green's Problem 49; its Bogolyubov-type analogue (Problem 50) remains open.

title: Schur's theorem with an explicit bound
q: Let $k\ge1$ and $N\ge\lfloor e\cdot k!\rfloor$. Prove that for every colouring of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $k$ colours there exist $x,y,z$ of the same colour (not necessarily distinct) with $x+y=z$.
source: I. Schur (1916); R. L. Graham, B. L. Rothschild and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley (1990)
note: Reduces to multicolour Ramsey numbers of triangles via the colouring of pairs by differences; gives the factorial upper bound in Erdős Problem 483.

title: The Schur number S(3) = 13
q: Show that $\{1,\ldots,13\}$ can be coloured with $3$ colours so that no colour class contains $x,y,z$ (not necessarily distinct) with $x+y=z$, but that every $3$-colouring of $\{1,\ldots,14\}$ contains such a monochromatic solution.
source: B. M. Landman and A. Robertson, Ramsey Theory on the Integers, AMS Student Mathematical Library (2004)
note: An exact small case, showing how far the general factorial bound is from the truth.

title: Exponential lower bound for Schur numbers
q: Let $S(k)$ be the largest $N$ such that $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ admits a $k$-colouring with no monochromatic solution of $x+y=z$ ($x,y$ not necessarily distinct). Prove that $S(k+1)\ge 3S(k)+1$ for every $k\ge1$, and deduce that $$S(k)\ge\frac{3^k-1}{2}.$$
source: I. Schur (1916); R. L. Graham, B. L. Rothschild and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley (1990)
note: The matching lower-bound construction; Erdős Problem 483 asks whether the true growth is exponential, i.e. whether $S(k)<c^k$.

title: Colourings that defeat a non-regular linear equation
q:
Let $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ be nonzero integers such that $\sum_{i\in I}a_i\neq0$ for every nonempty $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let $p$ be a prime with $p>\sum_{i=1}^k|a_i|$. Colour each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ by the last nonzero digit of $n$ in base $p$.

Prove that this colouring with $p-1$ colours has no monochromatic solution of $a_1x_1+\cdots+a_kx_k=0$.
source: R. Rado, Studien zur Kombinatorik, Math. Z. 36 (1933); R. L. Graham, B. L. Rothschild and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey Theory, 2nd ed. (1990)
note: The necessity half of Rado's theorem; the number of colours depends on the size of the coefficients, and Green's Problem 21 asks whether it can be bounded in terms of $k$ alone.

title: Van der Waerden's theorem
q: Prove that for all integers $k,r\ge1$ there exists $N$ such that every colouring of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $r$ colours contains a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length $k$.
source: B. L. van der Waerden, Beweis einer Baudetschen Vermutung, Nieuw Arch. Wisk. 15 (1927)
note: The colour-focusing induction, the engine behind Rado's sufficiency proof and finite-sums theorems.

title: Folkman's finite sums theorem
q: Prove that for all integers $r,m\ge1$ there exists $N$ such that for every $r$-colouring of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ there is a set $S$ of $m$ distinct positive integers such that all sums $\sum_{s\in T}s$, over nonempty $T\subseteq S$, lie in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and have the same colour.
source: J. Folkman, R. Rado, J. Sanders; R. L. Graham, B. L. Rothschild and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley (1990)
note: Finite version of Hindman's theorem; Erdős Problem 532 is the infinite version for two colours.

title: Rado's theorem for a single equation
q: Let $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ be nonzero integers. Prove that every finite colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ admits a monochromatic solution $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ of $$a_1x_1+\cdots+a_kx_k=0$$ if and only if $\sum_{i\in I}a_i=0$ for some nonempty $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$.
source: R. Rado, Studien zur Kombinatorik, Math. Z. 36 (1933)
note: Completes the characterisation of partition regular single equations; the boundedness question in Green's Problem 21 concerns the complementary case.

title: Rado's boundedness conjecture for three variables
q: Let $a_1,a_2,a_3$ be nonzero integers such that $\sum_{i\in I}a_i\neq0$ for every nonempty $I\subseteq\{1,2,3\}$. Prove that $\mathbb{N}$ can be coloured with $24$ colours so that there is no monochromatic solution of $$a_1x_1+a_2x_2+a_3x_3=0.$$
source: J. Fox and D. J. Kleitman, On Rado's boundedness conjecture, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 113 (2006), 84–100
note: The case $k=3$ of Green's Problem 21 with a bound independent of the coefficients; open for $k\ge4$.

title: Monochromatic x, x+y and xy
q: Prove that for every finite colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ there exist $x,y\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x$, $x+y$ and $xy$ all have the same colour.
source: J. Moreira, Monochromatic sums and products in N, Ann. of Math. 185 (2017), 1069–1090
note: Forces a sum and a product into one colour (together with $x$); Green's Problem 22 asks the same for the pair $x+y$, $xy$ alone (with $x,y\ge3$ to exclude $2+2=2\cdot2$), which remains open.

title: Partition regularity of Pythagorean pairs
q: Prove that for every finite colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ there exist distinct $x,y\in\mathbb{N}$ of the same colour such that $x^2+y^2$ is a perfect square.
source: N. Frantzikinakis, O. Klurman and J. Moreira, Partition regularity of Pythagorean pairs, Forum Math. Pi 13 (2025), e5, arXiv:2309.10636
note: Settles Green's Problem 23 via multiplicative functions; partition regularity of $x^2+y^2=z^2$ with $x,y,z$ all of one colour remains open for general finite colourings.

title: Discrepancy 1 survives exactly to length 11
q:
For $f:\{1,\ldots,N\}\to\{-1,1\}$ let $D(f)=\max\{|\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(kd)| : n,d\ge1,\ nd\le N\}$.

Show that some $f:\{1,\ldots,11\}\to\{-1,1\}$ has $D(f)=1$, but that every $f:\{1,\ldots,12\}\to\{-1,1\}$ has $D(f)\ge2$.
source: Folklore; the value 11 is a(1) in OEIS A237695 (maximum length of a ±1 sequence of discrepancy n), whose a(2)=1160 is due to B. Konev and A. Lisitsa, A SAT attack on the Erdős discrepancy conjecture, arXiv:1402.2184 (2014)
note: The case $C=1$ of the Erdős discrepancy problem by hand; the case $C=2$ already needed a SAT solver.

title: Weyl equidistribution and the quantifier in Khinchin's question
q:
Let $\alpha$ be irrational. Prove that for every interval $[a,b)\subseteq[0,1)$, $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\#\{1\le k\le n : \{k\alpha\}\in[a,b)\}=b-a.$$

Show on the other hand that for every real $\alpha$ there is a measurable $E\subseteq(0,1)$ with $\lambda(E)=1$ such that $\{k\alpha\}\notin E$ for all $k\ge1$.
source: H. Weyl, Über die Gleichverteilung von Zahlen mod. Eins, Math. Ann. 77 (1916); L. Kuipers and H. Niederreiter, Uniform Distribution of Sequences, Wiley (1974)
note: Equidistribution holds for intervals, but no single $\alpha$ works for all measurable sets, so Khinchin's question in Erdős Problem 994 must be read as: for each fixed $E$, for almost all $\alpha$.

title: Exponential sums of a sequence cannot all stay bounded
q: Let $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ be any sequence of real numbers and $e(t)=e^{2\pi it}$. Prove that $$\limsup_{k\to\infty}\ \sup_{n\ge1}\ \Big|\sum_{j=1}^{n}e(kx_j)\Big|=\infty.$$
source: Remark of P. Erdős (1964), recorded at erdosproblems.com/987 (where it is described as easy), together with the later results of Clunie (1967)
note: The version with $\sup_n$ is elementary; Erdős Problem 987 asks the same with $\limsup_n$ in place of $\sup_n$, and for the growth rate in $k$.

title: A multiplicative sequence with logarithmic discrepancy
q: Let $\lambda:\mathbb{N}\to\{-1,1\}$ be the completely multiplicative function with $\lambda(3)=1$, $\lambda(p)=1$ for primes $p\equiv1\pmod 3$ and $\lambda(p)=-1$ for primes $p\equiv2\pmod 3$. Prove that $$0\le\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lambda(k)\le\log_3 n+1\quad\text{for all } n\ge1,$$ and deduce that $|\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lambda(kd)|\le\log_3 N+1$ whenever $n,d\ge1$ and $nd\le N$.
source: P. Borwein, S. K. K. Choi and M. Coons, Completely multiplicative functions taking values in {−1,1}, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 362 (2010), 6279–6291 (Corollary 4)
note: Shows that discrepancy along homogeneous progressions can grow as slowly as $\log N$, matching the lower bound $\gg\log N$ that Erdős conjectured.

title: Random colourings of pairs: the upper bound n^{3/2}
q: For $f:\{(x,y): 1\le x<y\le n\}\to\{-1,1\}$ and $X\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ write $f(X)=\sum_{x<y,\ x,y\in X}f(x,y)$. Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every $n\ge1$ some $f$ satisfies $|f(X)|\le Cn^{3/2}$ for all $X\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$.
source: P. Erdős (1963), as recorded at erdosproblems.com/1028; the method is the standard Chernoff-plus-union-bound argument, see N. Alon and J. H. Spencer, The Probabilistic Method
note: Random colouring plus a union bound over all $2^n$ sets gives the upper bound in Erdős Problem 1028.

title: Roth's theorem on discrepancy in arithmetic progressions
q: Prove that there is a constant $c>0$ such that for every $N\ge1$ and every $f:\{1,\ldots,N\}\to\{-1,1\}$ there is an arithmetic progression $P\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $$\Big|\sum_{x\in P}f(x)\Big|\ge cN^{1/4}.$$
source: K. F. Roth, Remark concerning integer sequences, Acta Arith. 9 (1964); the exponent 1/4 is sharp by J. Matoušek and J. Spencer, Discrepancy in arithmetic progressions, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 9 (1996)
note: For all progressions (not only homogeneous ones) discrepancy is polynomial, in contrast with the logarithmic example above.

title: Erdős–Spencer lower bound for imbalance of 2-colourings of pairs
q: With $f(X)$ as above, prove that there is a constant $c>0$ such that for every $n\ge2$ and every $f:\{(x,y): 1\le x<y\le n\}\to\{-1,1\}$ there is $X\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $|f(X)|\ge cn^{3/2}$.
source: P. Erdős and J. Spencer, Imbalances in k-colorations, Networks 1 (1971/72), 379–385
note: Matches the random upper bound, giving $H(n)\asymp n^{3/2}$ in Erdős Problem 1028; the density version for large induced subgraphs is Erdős Problem 162.

title: Spencer's six standard deviations
q: Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every $n\ge1$ and any $n$ sets $S_1,\ldots,S_n\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ there exists $\chi:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{-1,1\}$ with $$\Big|\sum_{x\in S_i}\chi(x)\Big|\le C\sqrt n\quad\text{for all } 1\le i\le n.$$
source: J. Spencer, Six standard deviations suffice, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 289 (1985) (with $C=6$)
note: Beats random colouring (which gives $\sqrt{2n\log(2n)}$) by partial colouring and entropy; the prototype of all sharp discrepancy bounds.

title: Law of the iterated logarithm for lacunary exponential sums
q:
Let $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ be positive integers with $n_{k+1}/n_k\ge q$ for all $k$, for some fixed $q>1$. Prove that for almost every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, $$\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{|\sum_{k=1}^{N}e(n_k\alpha)|}{\sqrt{N\log\log N}}\le1.$$

Deduce that if $f$ is a trigonometric polynomial with $\int_0^1f=0$, then for almost every $\alpha$, $$\sum_{k=1}^{N}f(\{\alpha n_k\})=O\big(\sqrt{N\log\log N}\big),$$ and in particular this sum is $o(N\sqrt{\log\log N})$.
source: P. Erdős and I. S. Gál, On the law of the iterated logarithm I, II, Nederl. Akad. Wetensch. Proc. Ser. A 58 = Indag. Math. 17 (1955), 65–76, 77–84 (they prove the limsup equals 1)
note: Answers Erdős Problem 995 for trigonometric polynomials; the open case is general $f\in L^2$, where Erdős constructed examples whose sums exceed $N(\log\log N)^{1/2-\epsilon}$ infinitely often.

title: The Erdős discrepancy problem, Hilbert-space form
q:
Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and $f:\mathbb{N}\to H$ a function with $\|f(n)\|=1$ for all $n$. Prove that $$\sup_{n,d\ge1}\Big\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}f(jd)\Big\|=\infty.$$

In particular, every $f:\mathbb{N}\to\{-1,1\}$ has unbounded discrepancy along homogeneous arithmetic progressions.
source: T. Tao, The Erdős discrepancy problem, Discrete Analysis 2016:1, arXiv:1509.05363
note: Reduction to completely multiplicative functions plus a logarithmically averaged Elliott conjecture; the conjectured $\log N$ growth rate remains open.

title: The greedy Egyptian fraction algorithm terminates
q:
Let $0<\frac ab<1$ with $a,b$ positive integers. Let $n_1$ be the least positive integer with $\frac1{n_1}\le\frac ab$, replace $\frac ab$ by $\frac ab-\frac1{n_1}$, and repeat while the remainder is nonzero.

Prove that this process stops after at most $a$ steps, and that the denominators it produces are distinct, so that every rational number in $(0,1)$ is a finite sum of distinct unit fractions.
source: Fibonacci, Liber Abaci (1202); J. J. Sylvester, On a point in the theory of vulgar fractions, Amer. J. Math. 3 (1880), 332-335
note: The basic existence statement behind every question on the concept: representations always exist, so the problems are about their length, size and location.

title: Prime powers are never the largest denominator
q:
Suppose $1=\frac1{m_1}+\cdots+\frac1{m_k}$ with integers $1\le m_1<\cdots<m_k$ and $k\ge2$.

Prove that $m_k$ is not a prime power: if $p$ is a prime and $a\ge1$, then $m_k\neq p^a$.
source: Folklore; recorded as an easy remark at erdosproblems.com/292
note: A p-adic valuation argument that already shows the set of possible largest denominators misses infinitely many integers; the research question asks how large that exceptional set is.

title: Erdős–Straus outside one residue class mod 24
q:
Let $n>2$ be an integer with $n\not\equiv 1 \pmod{24}$.

Prove that there exist integers $1\le x<y<z$ with $$\frac4n=\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z.$$
source: Consequence of Mordell's parametric identities (L. J. Mordell, Diophantine Equations, Academic Press, 1969): every prime outside the classes 1, 121, 169, 289, 361, 529 mod 840 has a solution, and all of these classes are 1 mod 24; see erdosproblems.com/242 and C. Pomerance's survey notes
note: Explicit identities settle all but one residue class mod 24; this is why the conjecture is really about primes $p\equiv1 \pmod{24}$.

title: A lower bound for the largest denominator in a representation of 1
q:
For $k\ge1$ let $f(k)$ be the least possible value of $n_k$ over all integers $1\le n_1<\cdots<n_k$ with $\frac1{n_1}+\cdots+\frac1{n_k}=1$.

Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $k_0$ such that $f(k)\ge\left(\frac{e}{e-1}-\varepsilon\right)k$ for all $k\ge k_0$.
source: Trivial direction recorded at erdosproblems.com/285 (problem from P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory, 1980)
note: Comparing with $\sum_{N/e<n\le N}1/n\approx1$ gives the lower bound; the research problems ask that it be sharp, i.e. that $k$ denominators can be packed into an interval of width $(e-1+o(1))k$.

title: A large set with no subset of reciprocal sum 1
q: Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $N$ there is a set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $|A|\ge\left(1-\frac1e-\varepsilon\right)N$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\neq1$ for every nonempty $S\subseteq A$.
source: Folklore; stated as the trivial lower bound in Erdős Problem 300 and in Y. P. Liu and M. Sawhney, On further questions regarding unit fractions, arXiv:2404.07113 (2024)
note: An interval of integers whose reciprocals sum to slightly less than 1 gives the extremal example; the hard direction (rung below) shows no denser set works.

title: Erdős–Straus holds for almost all n
q:
For $N\ge2$ let $E(N)$ be the number of integers $2\le n\le N$ for which the equation $\frac4n=\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z$ has no solution in positive integers $x,y,z$.

Prove that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that $$E(N)\ll N\exp\!\left(-c(\log N)^{2/3}\right).$$
source: R. C. Vaughan, On a problem of Erdős, Straus and Schinzel, Mathematika 17 (1970), 193-198
note: Combining many parametric families with a sieve shows the exceptional set is very thin; the open problem asks that it be empty.

title: Almost every integer is the largest denominator of a representation of 1
q:
Let $A$ be the set of positive integers $n$ for which there exist integers $1\le m_1<\cdots<m_k=n$ with $\sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{m_i}=1$, and let $B=\mathbb N\setminus A$.

Prove that for all sufficiently large $x$ $$\#\{n\le x: n\in B\}\asymp\frac{x\log\log x}{\log x}.$$ In particular $A$ has natural density $1$.
source: G. Martin, Denser Egyptian fractions, Acta Arith. 95 (2000), no. 3; arXiv:math/9811112
note: Upgrades the prime-power obstruction rung to the true order of the exceptional set; the same paper determines the minimal largest denominator for $t$-term representations.

title: Croot's colouring theorem
q: Prove that for every integer $r\ge1$ there is an integer $N(r)$ with the following property: whenever $\{2,3,\ldots,N(r)\}$ is coloured with $r$ colours, there is a set $S$ of integers, all of the same colour, with $$\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=1.$$
source: E. S. Croot III, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions, Ann. of Math. (2) 157 (2003), no. 2, 545-556
note: Answers the Erdős–Graham colouring question; its method (finding many smooth denominators in one colour class) is the starting point for the density versions below.

title: Bloom's density theorem for unit fractions
q:
(a) Prove that there is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $N$, every $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $$\sum_{n\in A}\frac1n\ge C\,\frac{\log\log\log N}{\log\log N}\,\log N$$ contains a finite $S\subseteq A$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=1$.

(b) Prove that every $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ of positive upper density contains a finite $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=1$.
source: T. F. Bloom, On a density conjecture about unit fractions, arXiv:2112.03726 (2021)
note: Turns Croot's colouring method into a density result via a Fourier-analytic argument; a set with bounded gaps has positive density, and a stronger technical form of the theorem gives $(1-o(1))\log N$ disjoint representations of 1 inside $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

title: Liu–Sawhney: the sharp density threshold 1 - 1/e
q:
(a) Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $N$, every $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $\sum_{n\in A}\frac1n\ge(\log N)^{4/5+\varepsilon}$ contains a subset $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=1$.

(b) Prove that for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac12)$ and all sufficiently large $N$, every $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $|A|\ge\left(1-\frac1e+\varepsilon\right)N$ contains a subset $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=1$.
source: Y. P. Liu and M. Sawhney, On further questions regarding unit fractions, arXiv:2404.07113 (2024), Theorems 1.1 and 1.3
note: Part (b) matches the construction of the earlier rung, so the maximal size of a set with no subset of reciprocal sum 1 is $(1-1/e+o(1))N$; the same paper's refined method also treats denominators of $a/b$ and the quantity $t(N)$.

title: A covering system with distinct moduli
q:
(a) Prove that every integer satisfies at least one of the congruences $$x\equiv0\pmod2,\quad x\equiv0\pmod3,\quad x\equiv1\pmod4,\quad x\equiv5\pmod6,\quad x\equiv7\pmod{12}.$$

(b) Prove that if the congruences $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$, $1\le i\le k$, cover every integer, then $\sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{n_i}\ge1$, with equality if and only if every integer satisfies exactly one of them.
source: P. Erdős, On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems, Summa Brasil. Math. 2 (1950), 113-123
note: Erdős's original example and the density count used in every later argument about coverings.

title: Why 2^r consecutive integers are needed
q: Let $r\ge1$. Show that the $r$ congruences $x\equiv2^{i-1}\pmod{2^i}$, $1\le i\le r$, cover each of the $2^r-1$ consecutive integers $1,2,\ldots,2^r-1$ but do not cover all integers.
source: Folklore; given as the sharpness example in Erdős Problem 275
note: Shows the threshold $2^r$ in the Crittenden–Vanden Eynden theorem cannot be lowered.

title: A Sierpiński number from a covering
q:
(a) Prove that for every integer $n\ge0$ the number $78557\cdot2^n+1$ is divisible by at least one of the primes $3,5,7,13,19,37,73$, and hence is composite.

(b) Deduce, using the Chinese remainder theorem, that there are infinitely many odd $k$ for which $k\cdot2^n+1$ is composite for every $n\ge0$.
source: W. Sierpiński, Sur un problème concernant les nombres k·2^n+1, Elem. Math. 15 (1960), 73-74 (infinitely many such k); the example 78557 is due to J. Selfridge (1962, unpublished)
note: Each prime $p$ in the set handles one residue class of $n$ modulo the order of 2 mod $p$, so a covering system becomes a covering set; the research problems ask whether every such phenomenon must come from a covering.

title: No exact covering with distinct moduli
q:
Let $k\ge2$ and let $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$, $1\le i\le k$, be congruences with $1<n_1<n_2<\cdots<n_k$.

Prove that some integer satisfies none or at least two of these congruences. In fact, prove more: in any partition of $\mathbb Z$ into $k\ge2$ residue classes, the largest modulus occurs at least twice.
source: Mirsky and Newman, and independently Davenport and Rado (unpublished); reported in P. Erdős, On a problem concerning congruence systems, Mat. Lapok 3 (1952), 122-128
note: The generating-function proof uses $\sum_i z^{a_i}/(1-z^{n_i})=1/(1-z)$ and looks at a primitive $n_k$-th root of unity; this is the case $G=\mathbb Z$ of the coset-partition question.

title: r congruences covering 2^r consecutive integers cover everything
q: Let $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$, $1\le i\le r$, be $r$ congruences (the moduli need not be distinct). Prove that if every one of the integers $1,2,\ldots,2^r$ satisfies at least one of them, then every integer satisfies at least one of them.
source: R. B. Crittenden and C. L. Vanden Eynden, Any n arithmetic progressions covering the first 2^n integers cover all integers, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 24 (1970), 475–481
note: Together with the sharpness rung on 2^r consecutive integers this settles Erdős Problem 275 exactly.

title: Hough: the minimum modulus is bounded
q:
Call a finite set of congruences $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$ with distinct moduli $1<n_1<\cdots<n_k$ a distinct covering system if every integer satisfies at least one of them.

Prove that every distinct covering system has $n_1\le10^{16}$.
source: R. Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Ann. of Math. (2) 181 (2015), no. 1, 361-382
note: Answers Erdős's minimum modulus problem negatively using a probabilistic sieve with the Lovász local lemma.

title: The distortion method: Schinzel's question and a smaller minimum modulus
q:
(a) Prove that every distinct covering system has least modulus less than $10^6$.

(b) Prove that in every finite covering of $\mathbb Z$ by congruences $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$ with all $n_i>1$, there are $i\neq j$ with $n_i\mid n_j$.
source: P. Balister, B. Bollobás, R. Morris, J. Sahasrabudhe and M. Tiba, On the Erdős covering problem: the density of the uncovered set, Invent. Math. 228 (2022), no. 1, 377-414; arXiv:1811.03547
note: A simpler sieve that tracks the density of the uncovered set; part (b) closes Selfridge's route to an odd covering via moduli none of which divides another.

title: Every distinct covering has a modulus divisible by 2 or 3
q: Prove that in every distinct covering system (distinct moduli, all greater than 1, covering $\mathbb Z$) at least one modulus is divisible by $2$ or by $3$.
source: R. D. Hough and P. P. Nielsen, Covering systems with restricted divisibility, Duke Math. J. 168 (2019); arXiv:1703.02133
note: The strongest unconditional step towards the odd covering problem: an odd covering would need a modulus divisible by 3.

title: No odd square-free distinct covering
q: Prove that if a finite set of congruences $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$ with distinct square-free moduli $n_i>1$ covers $\mathbb Z$, then at least one $n_i$ is even.
source: P. Balister, B. Bollobás, R. Morris, J. Sahasrabudhe and M. Tiba, The Erdős–Selfridge problem with square-free moduli, Algebra Number Theory 15 (2021); arXiv:1901.11465
note: Settles the square-free case of the Erdős–Selfridge odd covering problem; the general odd case remains open.

title: Primitive subsets of {1, ..., 2n}
q:
A set $A$ of positive integers is primitive if no element of $A$ divides another element of $A$.

Prove that for every $n\ge1$ the largest primitive subset of $\{1,2,\ldots,2n\}$ has exactly $n$ elements.
source: Folklore (Erdős); see M. Aigner and G. M. Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK, chapter Pigeon-hole and double counting
note: Grouping by odd part gives the upper bound and $\{n+1,\ldots,2n\}$ the lower bound: counting alone cannot force primitive sets to be thin, which is why weighted sums are used.

title: Erdős's disjoint-multiples inequality
q:
For an integer $a\ge2$ let $P(a)$ be its largest prime factor and let $S_a$ be the set of integers $am$ with $m\ge1$ and every prime factor of $m$ at least $P(a)$.

Let $A\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}$ be primitive. Prove that the sets $S_a$ ($a\in A$) are pairwise disjoint, that $S_a$ has natural density $\frac1a\prod_{p<P(a)}\left(1-\frac1p\right)$ (product over primes), and deduce $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1a\prod_{p<P(a)}\left(1-\frac1p\right)\le1.$$
source: P. Erdős, Note on sequences of integers no one of which is divisible by any other, J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935), 126–128
note: The key inequality in Erdős's 1935 argument; the rest is Mertens' theorem.

title: Erdős: the sum of 1/(a log a) is uniformly bounded
q:
Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that every primitive set $A\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}$ satisfies $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{a\log a}\le C.$$

Deduce that every primitive set has lower asymptotic density $0$.
source: P. Erdős, Note on sequences of integers no one of which is divisible by any other, J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935), 126–128
note: Mertens' estimate $\prod_{p<y}(1-1/p)\asymp1/\log y$ applied to the previous rung; the primes show the sum can be about 1.6366, and the research problem asks whether that is the maximum.

title: Besicovitch: primitive sets can have positive upper density
q: Prove that there exists a primitive set $A\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}$ with positive upper asymptotic density, i.e. $$\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x}>0.$$
source: A. S. Besicovitch, On the density of certain sequences of integers, Math. Ann. 110 (1934/35), 336-341
note: Shows the previous rung cannot be upgraded to natural density zero; equivalently, sets of multiples need not have a natural density, which is why the Davenport–Erdős theory uses logarithmic density.

title: Davenport–Erdős: sets of multiples have logarithmic density
q:
Let $A$ be a set of positive integers and let $M(A)=\{am: a\in A,\ m\ge1\}$ be its set of multiples.

Prove that $M(A)$ has a logarithmic density, i.e. $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac1{\log x}\sum_{n\in M(A),\,n\le x}\frac1n$ exists, and that it equals the lower asymptotic density of $M(A)$.
source: H. Davenport and P. Erdős, On sequences of positive integers, Acta Arith. 2 (1936), 147-151; elementary proof in J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) 15 (1951), 19-24
note: The case $X_n=\{0\}$ of Erdős Problem 486; the open problem asks the same for an arbitrary choice of forbidden residues $X_n$.

title: Behrend's bound for reciprocal sums
q: Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that for all $x\ge3$ and every primitive set $A\subseteq\{2,\ldots,\lfloor x\rfloor\}$, $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1a\le C\frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}.$$
source: F. Behrend, On sequences of numbers not divisible one by another, J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935)
note: In particular primitive sets have logarithmic density zero; the real-number analogue of this bound is part of Erdős Problem 143.

title: The e^gamma bound
q: Prove that every primitive set $A\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}$ satisfies $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{a\log a}<e^{\gamma}=1.78107\ldots,$$ where $\gamma$ is Euler's constant.
source: J. D. Lichtman and C. Pomerance, The Erdős conjecture for primitive sets, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. Ser. B 6 (2019), 1-14; arXiv:1806.02250
note: Brings the universal bound within about 9 percent of the conjectured extremal value $\sum_p 1/(p\log p)=1.6366\ldots$.

title: Lichtman: the primes maximise the Erdős sum
q: Prove that every primitive set $A\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}$ satisfies $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{a\log a}\le\sum_{p\ \mathrm{prime}}\frac1{p\log p}.$$
source: J. D. Lichtman, A proof of the Erdős primitive set conjecture, Forum Math. Pi 11 (2023); arXiv:2202.02384
note: Resolves Erdős's conjecture; the translated version for primitive sets in $[x,\infty)$ and the real-number analogue are the next questions.

title: Bertrand's postulate
q: Prove that for every integer $n\ge 1$ there is a prime $p$ with $n<p\le 2n$. Deduce that $p_{n+1}<2p_n$ for every $n\ge 1$, where $p_n$ denotes the $n$th prime.
source: Aigner & Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK, Chapter 2 (Bertrand's postulate)
note: The first unconditional upper bound for prime gaps, proved by elementary estimates on the central binomial coefficient.

title: Average size and second moment of prime gaps
source: Elementary consequence of the prime number theorem (averaging and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality); the unconditional lower bound in (b) is stated at erdosproblems.com/233 (Erdős Problem #233)
note: Fixes the natural scale $\log p_n$ for gaps; (b) is the trivial lower bound matching Heath-Brown's conjectured upper bound $N(\log N)^2$.

title: Westzynthius: gaps are unboundedly larger than average
q:
Let $p_n$ denote the $n$th prime. Prove that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{\log p_n}=\infty.$$
source: E. Westzynthius, Über die Verteilung der Zahlen, die zu den n ersten Primzahlen teilerfremd sind, Societas Scientiarum Fennica, Commentationes Physico-Mathematicae 5 (1931), no. 25, 1–37
note: Shows that $\infty$ is a limit point of the normalized gaps, via long runs of integers each sharing a factor with the primorial.

title: Rankin's lower bound for large gaps
q:
Prove that there is a constant $c>0$ such that
$$p_{n+1}-p_n>c\,\frac{\log p_n\,\log\log p_n\,\log\log\log\log p_n}{(\log\log\log p_n)^2}$$
for infinitely many $n$.
source: R. A. Rankin, The difference between consecutive prime numbers, J. London Math. Soc. 13 (1938), 242–247
note: The Erdős–Rankin method: cover an interval by one residue class per small prime, using smooth numbers to handle the hardest part; Erdős Problem 4 asks to make $c$ arbitrarily large.

title: Long gaps between primes (Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao)
q:
Prove that for all sufficiently large $X$,
$$\max_{p_n\le X}(p_{n+1}-p_n)\gg\frac{\log X\,\log\log X\,\log\log\log\log X}{\log\log\log X}.$$
source: K. Ford, B. Green, S. Konyagin, J. Maynard, T. Tao, Long gaps between primes, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 31 (2018), 65–105
note: Gains a factor $\log\log\log X$ over Rankin (settling Erdős Problem 4 in a strong form) by combining the covering argument with Maynard's sieve weights; improving it further is the residue-class covering question of Green's Problem 46.

title: Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım: small normalized gaps
q:
Prove that
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{\log p_n}=0.$$
source: D. A. Goldston, J. Pintz, C. Y. Yıldırım, Primes in tuples I, Ann. of Math. (2) 170 (2009), 819–862
note: Shows that $0$ is a limit point of the normalized gaps, the case $C=0$ of Erdős Problem 5 (normalizing by $\log n$ or $\log p_n$ is equivalent).

title: Bounded gaps between primes (Maynard)
q: Prove that for every integer $m\ge 1$ there is a constant $C_m$ such that $p_{n+m}-p_n\le C_m$ for infinitely many $n$. In particular show that $p_{n+1}-p_n\le 600$ for infinitely many $n$.
source: J. Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Ann. of Math. (2) 181 (2015), 383–413
note: Multidimensional sieve weights give many primes in a single admissible tuple, which is the engine behind the solution of Erdős Problem 6 and the later rungs.

title: Monotone runs of prime gaps
q: Let $d_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$. Prove that for every $m\ge 1$ there are infinitely many $n$ with $d_n<d_{n+1}<\cdots<d_{n+m}$, and infinitely many $n$ with $d_n>d_{n+1}>\cdots>d_{n+m}$.
source: W. D. Banks, T. Freiberg, C. L. Turnage-Butterbaugh, Consecutive primes in tuples, Acta Arith. 167 (2015), no. 3, 261–266
note: Upgrades Maynard's theorem to control which members of a tuple are consecutive primes, settling the Erdős–Turán question (Erdős Problem 6); the same control over consecutive gaps is what Problems 852–853 ask about.

title: A positive proportion of limit points of normalized gaps
q: Let $L$ be the set of limit points in $[0,\infty)$ of the sequence $(p_{n+1}-p_n)/\log p_n$. Prove that for any nine real numbers $0\le\beta_1\le\beta_2\le\cdots\le\beta_9$, at least one difference $\beta_j-\beta_i$ with $1\le i<j\le 9$ lies in $L$. Deduce that the Lebesgue measure $\lambda$ satisfies $\lambda(L\cap[0,T])\ge(1-o(1))\,T/8$ as $T\to\infty$.
source: W. D. Banks, T. Freiberg, J. Maynard, On limit points of the sequence of normalized prime gaps, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 113 (2016), no. 4, 515–539, arXiv:1404.5094
note: The strongest type of result towards Erdős Problem 5 (whether every $C\ge0$ is a limit point); Merikoski (arXiv:1811.03008) later showed $\lambda(L\cap[0,T])\ge T/3$ for all $T$ and that $L$ has bounded gaps.

title: Strings of consecutive primes in one residue class (Shiu)
q: Let $q\ge 1$ and $a$ be integers with $\gcd(a,q)=1$, and let $k\ge 1$. Prove that there are infinitely many $r$ such that the $k$ consecutive primes $p_{r+1},p_{r+2},\ldots,p_{r+k}$ are all congruent to $a$ modulo $q$.
source: D. K. L. Shiu, Strings of congruent primes, J. London Math. Soc. (2) 61 (2000), 359–373
note: Answers Erdős Problem 427 (as observed on erdosproblems.com, a long string of consecutive primes $\equiv1\bmod d$ beyond $p_n$ lets the partial sums hit every residue class); it is the nearest proven statement to finding consecutive primes in arithmetic progression (Problem 141), where the differences, not just the residues, must be fixed.

title: Counting squarefree numbers
q:
Let $Q(x)$ be the number of squarefree positive integers $n\le x$. Prove that
$$Q(x)=\frac{6}{\pi^2}x+O(\sqrt{x}).$$
source: Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Ch. XVIII
note: The model computation: write the indicator of squarefree numbers as $\sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu(d)$ and sum.

title: No two elements with square product
q: For $N\ge1$ let $F_2(N)$ be the largest size of a set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that $ab$ is not a perfect square for any two distinct $a,b\in A$. Prove that $F_2(N)$ equals the number of squarefree integers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, so that $F_2(N)\sim\frac{6}{\pi^2}N$.
source: P. Erdős, A. Sárközy, V. T. Sós, On product representations of powers, I, European J. Combin. 16 (1995), 567–588
note: The case $k=2$ of the function $F_k(N)$ in Erdős Problem 121: square classes (squarefree kernels) are the right bookkeeping.

title: Structure and count of powerful numbers
q:
Call $n\ge1$ powerful if $p\mid n$ implies $p^2\mid n$ for every prime $p$. Prove that every powerful $n$ can be written uniquely as $n=a^2b^3$ with $a,b$ positive integers and $b$ squarefree. Deduce that the number $P(x)$ of powerful $n\le x$ satisfies
$$P(x)=\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)}\sqrt{x}+O(x^{1/3}).$$
source: S. W. Golomb, Powerful numbers, Amer. Math. Monthly 77 (1970), 848–852; the asymptotic goes back to P. Erdős and G. Szekeres, Acta Sci. Math. (Szeged) 7 (1934), 95–102
note: Gives the density of powerful numbers (about $\sqrt{x}$ of them up to $x$), the heuristic baseline for every question about consecutive or additive patterns of powerful numbers.

title: Consecutive powerful numbers
q:
(a) Prove that there are no four consecutive positive integers that are all powerful.

(b) Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $n$ and $n+1$ are both powerful.
source: S. W. Golomb, Powerful numbers, Amer. Math. Monthly 77 (1970), 848–852
note: Pairs are plentiful via Pell equations and quadruples are impossible mod 4; triples (Erdős Problem 364) sit exactly between what is easy in both directions.

title: Smooth numbers with one large prime factor
q:
Let $\Psi(x,y)$ be the number of $n\le x$ all of whose prime factors are at most $y$. Using Mertens' theorem, prove that for each fixed $u\in[1,2]$,
$$\Psi(x,x^{1/u})=(1-\log u)\,x+O\Big(\frac{x}{\log x}\Big)\quad(x\to\infty).$$
source: Tenenbaum, Introduction to Analytic and Probabilistic Number Theory, Ch. III.5 (Integers free of large prime factors)
note: Computes Dickman's function on $[1,2]$, where $\rho(u)=1-\log u$, by an inclusion-exclusion that uses only one large prime factor.

title: Consecutive powerful numbers, neither a square
q: Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $n$ and $n+1$ are both powerful and neither $n$ nor $n+1$ is a perfect square.
source: D. T. Walker, Consecutive integer pairs of powerful numbers and related Diophantine equations, Fibonacci Quart. 14 (1976), no. 2, 111–116
note: Gives infinitely many counterexamples to part (a) of Erdős Problem 365 (Golomb had found $23^3$, $23^3+1$); part (b), the $(\log x)^{O(1)}$ count, remains open.

title: Dickman's theorem
q:
Let $\rho:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be the continuous function with $\rho(u)=1$ for $0<u\le1$ and $u\rho'(u)=-\rho(u-1)$ for $u>1$. Prove that for each fixed $u\ge1$,
$$\Psi(x,x^{1/u})\sim\rho(u)\,x\quad(x\to\infty).$$
source: K. Dickman, On the frequency of numbers containing prime factors of a certain relative magnitude, Ark. Mat. Astr. Fys. 22A (1930), no. 10, 1–14
note: Extends the previous rung to all $u$ by an integral-delay recursion; smooth-number counts like this drive the large-gap constructions in prime-patterns.

title: Products of consecutive integers are never powers (Erdős–Selfridge)
q: Prove that for integers $n\ge1$, $k\ge2$ and $\ell\ge2$, the product $n(n+1)\cdots(n+k-1)$ is never an $\ell$th power of an integer.
source: P. Erdős, J. L. Selfridge, The product of consecutive integers is never a power, Illinois J. Math. 19 (1975), 292–301
note: Erdős Problem 137 asks for the much weaker conclusion 'never powerful' for $k\ge3$, which is open even though 'never a perfect power' is known.

title: Coprime arithmetic progressions of powerful numbers
q: Prove that there are infinitely many pairs of positive integers $(N,d)$ with $\gcd(N,d)=1$ such that $N,N+d,N+2d,N+3d$ are all powerful. Prove also that there are infinitely many such pairs with $\gcd(N,d)=1$ for which $N,N+d,N+2d$ are all $3$-full (every prime factor occurs to at least the third power).
source: P. Bajpai, M. A. Bennett, T. H. Chan, Arithmetic progressions in squarefull numbers, Int. J. Number Theory 20 (2024), no. 1, 19–45, arXiv:2302.03113
note: Resolves Erdős Problem 937; without coprimality the problem is trivial (scale any progression by a suitable square), and the same paper shows under abc that these lengths are optimal.

title: Five elements with square product (Tao)
q: For $N\ge1$ let $F_5(N)$ be the largest size of a set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that no product of five distinct elements of $A$ is a perfect square. Prove that there is a constant $c>0$ such that $F_5(N)\le(1-c+o(1))N$ as $N\to\infty$.
source: T. Tao, On product representations of squares, arXiv:2405.11610 (2024)
note: Answers Erdős Problem 121 in the negative (the conjecture was $F_5(N)=(1-o(1))N$), contrasting with $F_3(N)=(1-o(1))N$ proved by Erdős–Sárközy–Sós.

title: Dirichlet's approximation theorem
q:
Let $\alpha$ be an irrational real number. Prove that there are infinitely many pairs of integers $(p,q)$ with $q\ge1$ such that
$$\Big|\alpha-\frac{p}{q}\Big|<\frac{1}{q^2}.$$
source: Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Ch. XI
note: The baseline exponent $2$ that every later rung either improves on (for special numbers) or shows to be essentially optimal.

title: Liouville's inequality
q:
Let $\alpha$ be a real algebraic number of degree $d\ge2$. Prove that there is a constant $c(\alpha)>0$ such that
$$\Big|\alpha-\frac{p}{q}\Big|>\frac{c(\alpha)}{q^d}$$
for all integers $p$ and $q\ge1$. Deduce that $\sum_{n\ge1}10^{-n!}$ is transcendental.
source: Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Ch. XI
note: The basic mechanism of irrationality and transcendence proofs: a number with too-good rational approximations cannot be rational or algebraic of low degree.

title: Khintchine's theorem
q: For real $x$ let $\|x\|$ be the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer. Let $\psi:\mathbb{N}\to[0,\infty)$ be non-increasing. Prove that if $\sum_{q\ge1}\psi(q)<\infty$ then for almost every $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ the inequality $\|q\alpha\|<\psi(q)$ has only finitely many solutions $q\in\mathbb{N}$, while if $\sum_{q\ge1}\psi(q)=\infty$ then for almost every $\alpha$ it has infinitely many solutions.
source: A. Khintchine, Einige Sätze über Kettenbrüche, mit Anwendungen auf die Theorie der Diophantischen Approximationen, Math. Ann. 92 (1924), 115–125
note: The convergence half is Borel–Cantelli; the divergence half needs monotonicity, and removing it (with coprimality) is exactly the Duffin–Schaeffer problem.

title: Irrationality of the Lambert series at 1/2 (Erdős)
q:
Prove that
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{2^n-1}=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\tau(n)}{2^n}$$
is irrational, where $\tau(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$.
source: P. Erdős, On arithmetical properties of Lambert series, J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) 12 (1948), 63–66
note: The case $A=\mathbb{N}$ of Erdős Problem 257 and the case $t=2$ of Problem 1049: the binary expansion of the sum is controlled by the divisor function.

title: Borwein's irrationality of q-harmonic type series
q:
Let $q\ge2$ be an integer and $r\ne0$ a rational number with $r\ne-q^n$ for all $n\ge1$. Prove that
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{q^n+r}$$
is irrational.
source: P. B. Borwein, On the irrationality of Σ 1/(q^n+r), J. Number Theory 37 (1991), 253–259
note: Settles Erdős Problem 1050 ($q=2$, $r=-3$) via Padé approximation and also recovers the integer-$t$ case of Problem 1049 (first proved by Erdős in 1948); the rational non-integer $t$ case of 1049 stays open.

title: Roth's theorem
q:
Let $\alpha$ be a real algebraic irrational number and $\varepsilon>0$. Prove that there are only finitely many pairs of integers $(p,q)$ with $q\ge1$ such that
$$\Big|\alpha-\frac{p}{q}\Big|<\frac{1}{q^{2+\varepsilon}}.$$
source: K. F. Roth, Rational approximations to algebraic numbers, Mathematika 2 (1955), 1–20
note: Shows Dirichlet's exponent $2$ is sharp for every algebraic irrational, improving Liouville's $d$ all the way down.

title: Littlewood's conjecture for cubic fields (Cassels–Swinnerton-Dyer)
q:
For real $x$ let $\|x\|$ be the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer. Let $K$ be a real cubic number field and let $\alpha,\beta\in K$ be such that $1,\alpha,\beta$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. Prove that
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}n\,\|n\alpha\|\,\|n\beta\|=0.$$
source: J. W. S. Cassels, H. P. F. Swinnerton-Dyer, On the product of three homogeneous linear forms and indefinite ternary quadratic forms, Philos. Trans. Roy. Soc. London Ser. A 248 (1955), 73–96
note: Littlewood's conjecture is trivial unless both $\alpha,\beta$ are badly approximable; cubic pairs are the most natural such pairs, and this is the case proved.

title: The Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture (Koukoulopoulos–Maynard)
q:
Let $\psi:\mathbb{N}\to[0,\infty)$ be any function and let $\varphi$ be Euler's totient function. Prove that for almost every $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ the inequality
$$\Big|\alpha-\frac{a}{q}\Big|<\frac{\psi(q)}{q}$$
has infinitely many solutions in integers $a,q$ with $q\ge1$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$ if and only if $\sum_{q\ge1}\varphi(q)\psi(q)/q=\infty$.
source: D. Koukoulopoulos, J. Maynard, On the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture, Ann. of Math. (2) 192 (2020), 251–307
note: Removes the monotonicity hypothesis from Khintchine's theorem (with reduced fractions), resolving Erdős Problem 999.

title: Exceptions to Littlewood have dimension zero (Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss)
q:
For real $x$ let $\|x\|$ be the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer. Prove that the set of pairs $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}n\,\|n\alpha\|\,\|n\beta\|>0$$
has Hausdorff dimension $0$.
source: M. Einsiedler, A. Katok, E. Lindenstrauss, Invariant measures and the set of exceptions to Littlewood's conjecture, Ann. of Math. (2) 164 (2006), 513–560
note: The strongest known result toward the Littlewood conjecture (Erdős Problem 495), obtained by measure rigidity for diagonal actions on $\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$.

title: Irrationality of the sum over primes (Tao–Teräväinen)
q:
Let $\omega(n)$ be the number of distinct prime factors of $n$. Prove that
$$\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\omega(n)}{2^n}=\sum_{p\ \mathrm{prime}}\frac{1}{2^p-1}$$
(verify this identity first) and that this number is irrational.
source: T. Tao, J. Teräväinen, Quantitative correlations and some problems on prime factors of consecutive integers, arXiv:2512.01739 (2025)
note: Settles Erdős Problem 69 and the case $A=$ primes of Problem 257, extending Erdős's $A=\mathbb{N}$ rung; it needs correlation estimates for $\omega(n)$ and $\omega(n+h)$ in place of the divisor-function structure.

title: Few edges force property B
q:
Let $n\ge 1$ and let $H$ be an $n$-uniform hypergraph (every edge has exactly $n$ vertices) with fewer than $2^{n-1}$ edges.

Prove that the vertices of $H$ can be coloured red and blue so that no edge is monochromatic. Deduce that $m(n)\ge 2^{n-1}$, where $m(n)$ is the least number of edges of an $n$-uniform hypergraph that is not $2$-colourable.
source: P. Erdős, On a combinatorial problem, Nordisk Mat. Tidskr. 11 (1963); Alon & Spencer, The Probabilistic Method (chapter on property B)
note: The one-line first-moment argument gives the starting lower bound for the property B function $m(n)$.

title: Turán's construction for the tetrahedron
q:
Partition a set $V$ of $n$ vertices into three parts $V_0,V_1,V_2$ whose sizes differ by at most $1$. Let $H$ be the $3$-uniform hypergraph on $V$ whose edges are the triples meeting all three parts, together with the triples having two vertices in $V_i$ and one vertex in $V_{i+1}$ (indices mod $3$), for $i=0,1,2$.

(a) Prove that no $4$ vertices of $H$ span all $4$ possible triples, i.e. $H$ contains no $K_4^{(3)}$.

(b) Prove that $H$ has $\left(\frac59+o(1)\right)\binom n3$ edges as $n\to\infty$.

(c) Show by averaging over $4$-sets that every $K_4^{(3)}$-free $3$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices has at most $\frac34\binom n3$ edges.
source: P. Keevash, Hypergraph Turán problems, Surveys in Combinatorics 2011 (LMS Lecture Note Ser. 392)
note: Gives the conjectured extremal example and a trivial upper bound, framing the gap $[5/9,3/4]$ that the rest of the ladder narrows.

title: Random lower bound for 3-uniform Ramsey numbers
q:
Let $R_3(n)$ be the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the $3$-element subsets of an $N$-element set contains $n$ points all of whose triples have the same colour.

Prove that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that $R_3(n)>2^{cn^2}$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
source: Graham, Rothschild & Spencer, Ramsey Theory (2nd ed., 1990)
note: The random colouring gives only $2^{cn^2}$, while the Erdős–Rado upper bound is $2^{2^{Cn}}$; closing this gap for two colours is exactly Erdős Problem 564.

title: Graphs with no s+1 disjoint edges
q:
Let $s\ge 1$ and $n\ge 2s+2$. Prove that a graph on $n$ vertices containing no $s+1$ pairwise disjoint edges has at most
$$\max\left\{\binom{2s+1}{2},\ \binom n2-\binom{n-s}{2}\right\}$$
edges, and that this bound is attained.
source: P. Erdős and T. Gallai, On maximal paths and circuits of graphs, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 10 (1959)
note: This is the $r=2$ case of the Erdős matching problem $f(n;r,k)$: the two extremal families (a clique, or all edges meeting a fixed $s$-set) are exactly the conjectured ones for all $r$.

title: Complete r-partite r-graphs have Turán density zero
q:
For $r\ge 2$ and $s\ge 1$ let $K_r(s)$ be the complete $r$-partite $r$-uniform hypergraph with $s$ vertices in each class.

Prove that there is $n_0(r,s)$ such that for all $n\ge n_0$ every $r$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices with at least $n^{\,r-s^{1-r}}$ edges contains a copy of $K_r(s)$. Deduce that an $r$-uniform hypergraph $F$ satisfies $\mathrm{ex}_r(n,F)=o(n^r)$ if and only if $F$ is $r$-partite.
source: P. Erdős, On extremal problems of graphs and generalized graphs, Israel J. Math. 2 (1964)
note: Extends Kővári–Sós–Turán to hypergraphs; Erdős Problem 1158 asks whether the exponent $r-s^{1-r}$ is sharp, and the result also shows $0$ is a jump.

title: The (6,3) theorem
q:
Let $H$ be a $3$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices in which no $6$ vertices span $3$ or more edges.

Prove that $H$ has $o(n^2)$ edges as $n\to\infty$.
source: I. Z. Ruzsa and E. Szemerédi, Triple systems with no six points carrying three triangles, Colloq. Math. Soc. János Bolyai 18 (1978)
note: This is the case $r=3$, $e=3$ of the Brown–Erdős–Sós problem; it settles Erdős Problem 716, and Problem 1178 asks for the analogue for every $e$ and $r$.

title: Erdős matching conjecture for large n
q:
Let $k\ge 2$, $s\ge 1$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a family of $k$-element subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ containing no $s+1$ pairwise disjoint members.

Prove that if $n\ge (2s+1)k-s$ then
$$|\mathcal F|\le \binom nk-\binom{n-s}{k}.$$
source: P. Frankl, Improved bounds for Erdős' matching conjecture, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 120 (2013)
note: Confirms the conjectured value of $f(n;k,s+1)$ in a linear range of $n$; the conjecture predicts $\max\{\binom{(s+1)k-1}{k},\binom nk-\binom{n-s}{k}\}$ for all $n\ge (s+1)k$.

title: Improved lower bound for property B
q:
Let $m(n)$ be the least number of edges of an $n$-uniform hypergraph that is not $2$-colourable.

Prove that
$$m(n)=\Omega\!\left(2^n\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}\right).$$
source: J. Radhakrishnan and A. Srinivasan, Improved bounds and algorithms for hypergraph 2-coloring, Random Structures Algorithms 16 (2000)
note: Improves the easy $2^{n-1}$ by a factor $\sqrt{n/\log n}$; Erdős's random construction gives $m(n)=O(n^2 2^n)$, and the true order is Problem 901.

title: Hypergraphs do not jump
q:
For $r\ge 3$, call $\alpha\in[0,1)$ a jump for $r$ if there is $c>0$ such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every integer $m\ge r$ there is $n_0(\varepsilon,m)$ such that every $r$-uniform hypergraph on $n>n_0$ vertices with at least $(\alpha+\varepsilon)\binom nr$ edges contains a subhypergraph on $m$ vertices with at least $(\alpha+c)\binom mr$ edges.

Prove that for every $r\ge 3$ and every integer $l>2r$, the number $1-\frac{1}{l^{\,r-1}}$ is not a jump for $r$.
source: P. Frankl and V. Rödl, Hypergraphs do not jump, Combinatorica 4 (1984)
note: Erdős proved every $\alpha\in[0,r!/r^r)$ is a jump; Frankl–Rödl disproved that every $\alpha$ is, leaving open whether $r!/r^r$ itself is a jump (the question behind Problem 1075); Problem 837 asks for the full set of jumps when $r=3$.

title: Flag-algebra bound for the tetrahedron
q: Prove that for all sufficiently large $n$, every $3$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices containing no $K_4^{(3)}$ (four vertices spanning all four triples) has at most $0.562\binom n3$ edges.
source: A. A. Razborov, On 3-hypergraphs with forbidden 4-vertex configurations, SIAM J. Discrete Math. 24 (2010)
note: Razborov's flag-algebra computation was the first to push the upper bound well below the averaging bound $3/4$, towards Turán's conjectured $5/9\approx 0.5556$; Baber later lowered it to $0.5615$, and a 2026 preprint claims $0.5578$.

title: Mantel's theorem
q: Prove that a graph on $n$ vertices containing no triangle has at most $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ edges, and determine all graphs attaining this bound.
source: B. Bollobás, Extremal Graph Theory (1978); Aigner & Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK
note: This is the base case of Turán's theorem and the first instance of an exact extremal number.

title: Kővári–Sós–Turán bound
q:
Let $1\le s\le t$ be integers. Prove that every graph on $n$ vertices with no subgraph isomorphic to $K_{s,t}$ has at most
$$\frac12 (t-1)^{1/s}\, n^{2-1/s}+\frac12 (s-1)\,n$$
edges.
source: T. Kővári, V. T. Sós and P. Turán, On a problem of K. Zarankiewicz, Colloq. Math. 3 (1954); see Bollobás, Extremal Graph Theory
note: Gives the upper bound $\mathrm{ex}(n;K_{r,r})=O(n^{2-1/r})$ whose matching lower bound is Erdős Problem 714.

title: The asymptotics of ex(n, C4)
q:
Prove that
$$\mathrm{ex}(n;C_4)=\left(\tfrac12+o(1)\right)n^{3/2}\qquad(n\to\infty).$$

For the lower bound, for a prime power $q$ take as vertices the points of the projective plane over $\mathbb F_q$ and join distinct points $(x_0:x_1:x_2)$ and $(y_0:y_1:y_2)$ when $x_0y_0+x_1y_1+x_2y_2=0$; then use the density of primes to pass to all $n$.
source: P. Erdős, A. Rényi and V. T. Sós, On a problem of graph theory, Studia Sci. Math. Hungar. 1 (1966); W. G. Brown, On graphs that do not contain a Thomsen graph, Canad. Math. Bull. 9 (1966)
note: The first bipartite extremal number known asymptotically; Füredi later found the exact value for $n=q^2+q+1$, which answers Problem 765.

title: Erdős–Stone–Simonovits
q:
Let $H$ be a graph with chromatic number $\chi(H)=r+1\ge 2$. Prove that
$$\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=\left(1-\frac1r+o(1)\right)\binom n2 .$$

In particular, conclude that $\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=o(n^2)$ if and only if $H$ is bipartite.
source: P. Erdős and A. H. Stone, On the structure of linear graphs, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 52 (1946); P. Erdős and M. Simonovits, A limit theorem in graph theory, Studia Sci. Math. Hungar. 1 (1966)
note: Settles the non-bipartite case to first order, so every remaining question about the order of magnitude of $\mathrm{ex}(n;H)$ concerns bipartite $H$.

title: A dense K_{3,3}-free graph
q: Prove that there is a constant $c>0$ such that for all $n\ge 2$ there is a graph on $n$ vertices with at least $c\,n^{5/3}$ edges and no subgraph isomorphic to $K_{3,3}$.
source: W. G. Brown, On graphs that do not contain a Thomsen graph, Canad. Math. Bull. 9 (1966)
note: This is the case $r=3$ of Problem 714 (the case $r=2$ is the $C_4$ rung); Brown's construction uses spheres in $\mathbb F_p^3$, and the case $r\ge 4$ is open.

title: Even cycles: the Bondy–Simonovits bound
q: Let $k\ge 2$. Prove that there is a constant $C_k$ such that every graph on $n$ vertices with no cycle of length exactly $2k$ has at most $C_k\, n^{1+1/k}$ edges.
source: J. A. Bondy and M. Simonovits, Cycles of even length in graphs, J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 16 (1974)
note: Gives the upper bound that Problem 572 asks to match from below.

title: Dense graphs with no 6-cycle
q: Prove that there is a constant $c>0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ there is a graph on $n$ vertices with at least $c\,n^{4/3}$ edges and no cycle of length $6$.
source: C. T. Benson, Minimal regular graphs of girths eight and twelve, Canad. J. Math. 18 (1966); R. Wenger, Extremal graphs with no C4's, C6's, or C10's, J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 52 (1991)
note: This is the case $k=3$ of Problem 572, from incidence graphs of generalized quadrangles; the matching lower bound is known only for $k\in\{2,3,5\}$.

title: Norm graphs
q:
Let $t\ge 2$ and $s\ge (t-1)!+1$ be integers. Prove that there is $c=c(t,s)>0$ such that
$$\mathrm{ex}(n;K_{t,s})\ge c\,n^{2-1/t}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.
